added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: markets don't care about that uh, till they kind of do
added_claims.claim: Governmental and institutional changes are ignored by markets until they have structural effects, and Jem expects them to accelerate into the 2026 midterms and become a market focus.

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: the risks and the things counteracting those risks are bigger
added_claims.claim: Compared with 1998-99 the risks are bigger but so are the counter-forces: stronger government control and a larger toolset, plus market structure (structured products, flows into non-correlated vehicles) that reflexively supports prices.
added_claims.conditions: Government willing to act regardless of inflation

added_claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
added_claims.quote: the market continues higher and and and and by and that improves the fundamentals until they see the flow
added_claims.claim: Soros-style reflexivity: participants misjudge a flaw, prices keep rising, and the rise improves the fundamentals (for example higher valuations financing AI spend) until the flaw is finally recognised.

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: liquidity you manage the market because that's actually the greatest source of liquidity in the world
added_claims.claim: The Fed's claim that it does not manage the market is hollow, since markets are themselves the greatest source of liquidity; managing liquidity therefore manages the market, and a 20% rise creates more liquidity than QE.
added_claims.testable: partly - collateral and credit growth are measurable

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: when VA is very well supplied to the market despite liquidity being pulled from the market it could it stabilizes things
added_claims.claim: Volatility selling (structured products, vol supply) stabilises markets even when central-bank liquidity is withdrawn and allows other liquidity to return, which can delay the end of a rally.
added_claims.testable: partly - volatility supply is not directly measurable

added_claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
added_claims.quote: which resulted in the great moderation um and low interest rates came down and they came down so far that central banks and government started to borrow excessively
added_claims.claim: Central-bank independence produced the Great Moderation and very low rates, which let governments borrow excessively and now lead people to give up that independence, an example of one regime creating the next.

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: takes a long time to build trust. It takes very little to lose trust.
added_claims.claim: Confidence in US institutions (rule of law, central-bank credibility, 'shining city on a hill') is eroding and is hard to rebuild, and Jem sees this as only the beginning of a loss of faith.

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: we started talking about this a couple months ago as being the next big trade, meaning year, multi-year trade
added_claims.claim: Long-dated right-tail call pricing was Jem's multi-year trade idea two months earlier and has since exploded higher in the last month, which he sees as the first inning of repricing.

added_claims.speaker: Jem
added_claims.quote: we have very strict rules around healthcare data. Data is locked up sequestered in very unique places and very hard to access.
added_claims.claim: Healthcare is inefficient because strict data-privacy rules lock up data, so owners of large unique healthcare data sets (such as UnitedHealth) hold undervalued AI-relevant assets.

added_claims.claim: A calendar event risk for the end of 2025: Supreme Court arguments on the tariffs in November with a ruling afterwards.

added_claims.claim: Full political control of the Fed arrives in May (end of Powell's term) and markets already know it, so expected liquidity is on the way while institutions are caught underweight.

corrections.issue: Speaker mixed: the deficit, tariffs and productivity differences are Alan's; the loss of US hegemony (USSR had just fallen, no rival in 1998) and the bigger government toolset are Jem's.
corrections.fix: Alan: unlike 1999 the US has a deficit rather than a surplus, tariffs are in play and productivity growth is weaker. Jem: in 1998 the US was the unrivalled hegemon after the USSR fell, which is no longer true, yet government has more control and tools today.

corrections.issue: The claim text is garbled and contains a question mark. Jem says owning the stock means owning the whole distribution (short the left tail, underweight the right tail), and that the right tail is the cheapest part to replace it with.
corrections.fix: Replace stock with out-of-the-money long-dated calls (e.g. a 112% strike, a year or four to six months out, against average long-term volatility of about 17): the right tail is the cheapest part of the distribution and owning stock leaves the holder carrying the left tail.

corrections.issue: Strength of the statement understated: Jem says fundamentals have 'zero predictive value over any period less than 10 years' (not 'little').
corrections.fix: Valuations are not a timing tool: Jem says fundamentals have zero predictive value over periods under 10 years but become much more predictive beyond 10 years, so valuation is a risk-management gauge (distance from the ground), not a sell signal.

corrections.issue: Speaker: the point that autocallable-type structures mean investors are net sellers of volatility is raised by Alan and confirmed by Jem ('that's very correct').
corrections.fix: Alan observes that autocallable-type structured products are mostly short volatility; Jem confirms and says the 2 trillion total also includes ETFs and buffer products issuing similar structures.

completeness_estimate: 0.87 - first reader (51 claims) captured the bubble, structured-product, positioning, year-end flow and options-skew arguments well; misses are secondary mechanisms (vol supply stabilising, Fed managing liquidity), a few reasoning steps, and speaker attributions.
